title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 176
paragraphs: As for Artemisium first: coming out of the Thracian Sea, the open waters contract from great width to the narrow channel that lies between the island of Sciathos and the mainland of Magnesia; and after the strait there follows immediately, on Euboea, the beach called Artemisium, on which stands a temple of Artemis. Secondly, the passage into Greece by Trachis is, where it is narrowest, about fifty feet wide; but this is not the narrowest part of the whole region. That lies in front of Thermopylae and also behind it: at Alpeni, which lies behind Thermopylae, and again at the river Phoenix near the town of Anthela, the road is only a single wheel-track wide. On the west of Thermopylae there is a mountain impassable and sheer, rising to a great height and extending toward the range of Oeta, while on the east of the road the sea with its marshy pools comes up right against it. In this pass there are hot springs, which the natives call the “Pots,” and an altar of Heracles is set up near them. A wall had once been built at this pass, and in old times there was a gate set in it; this wall was built by the Phocians out of fear, because the Thessalians had come from the land of the Thesprotians to settle in the Aeolian land that they now occupy. Since the Thessalians, as they supposed, were trying to subdue them, the Phocians guarded themselves against this in advance; and at that time they also let the water of the hot springs run over the passage, to turn the place into a ravine, and contrived every possible means that the Thessalians should not invade their land. The old wall had been built long before and was by now mostly fallen into ruin with age. The Greeks resolved to set it up again, and at this spot to repel the barbarian from Greece. Very close to the road is a village called Alpeni, from which the Greeks counted on getting their supplies.
